# v3.04

This stable release rolls up dev pre-releases v3.01-dev, v3.02-dev, v3.03-dev and
v3.04-dev. It is a security and robustness release throughout; **updating promptly
is recommended**.

**One change needs action from you, and only if you email scheduled reports
through a mail server with a self-signed certificate.** See Upgrading at the end.

## Sessions and accounts

- **Deleting a user now ends any session that person already has open.**
  Previously the account disappeared from the Users page while their browser
  carried on working — with their old role and their old access — until the
  session eventually timed out. For someone still using the app that could be the
  rest of the working day, because ordinary activity kept extending it. Their next
  action is now refused and they are signed out cleanly, exactly as disabling an
  account already worked, and the two are indistinguishable from outside.

  This also covers the background keep-alive an open tab sends, which had been
  quietly preventing a deleted account's session from ever expiring on its own.

- **Creating or restoring an account is unaffected.** A new user can sign in and
  start work immediately, and sessions already in progress are untouched. If the
  database is briefly unavailable nobody is signed out — the check deliberately
  errs towards keeping everyone working rather than locking out the whole system
  over a momentary hiccup.

## Backup and restore

- **Restored accounts can no longer be handed a live session by an old archive.**
  A restore rebuilds the accounts table, and each restored account used to take
  the session marker recorded inside the archive — usually an older, lower value
  than the one in use. Every restored account now starts above every marker that
  existed before the restore.

- **An archive is refused if its contents would unpack to more than a set
  ceiling.** The previous limit applied to the file as it arrived, not to what it
  expands into, so a small file crafted to unpack enormously could exhaust the
  server's memory part-way through a restore. Real backups are stored unpacked and
  sit far below the ceiling.

- **Restoring from the backups folder now respects the same file-size limit as an
  uploaded file.** That path had no limit at all.

- **Passphrases for new portable backups must be at least 12 characters**, up from
  8. Portable backups you already hold are unaffected and still restore with the
  passphrase they were created with.

## Scheduled exports

- **Training Tracker now verifies your mail server's certificate before handing
  over the SMTP password.** It previously accepted any certificate from any
  server. There is a new **Allow self-signed certificate** tickbox for
  installations that need it — see Upgrading.

- **Provider credentials are validated when you save them.** The SMTP host must be
  a hostname or an IP address and the port a number between 1 and 65535, so a typo
  is reported immediately instead of surfacing days later as a report that never
  arrived. Only the settings a provider actually uses can be stored, and the
  OneDrive tenant ID is checked against a strict format — it could previously
  contain characters that reshaped the sign-in request.

- **Saving a credential now tells you what was wrong**, rather than the same
  "failed to save" message whatever the cause.

- **Emailing a report gives up after a few seconds** when the mail server cannot
  be reached, instead of waiting around two minutes on every attempt.

## Configuration and startup

- **Training Tracker now checks its own configuration when it starts.** Anything
  missing or malformed is named in the startup log with what to set and where. A
  missing database address or session secret is reported plainly, instead of the
  application starting normally and then failing with an unexplained error the
  first time somebody tried to sign in.

  If that happens, note what it looks like: the service keeps running and the port
  stays open, and only pages and data requests fail. **Do not judge it by the
  service status — read the log.**

- **Two silent failures now announce themselves.** Without the encryption key,
  stored mail passwords and authenticator secrets were being written to the
  database unencrypted with nothing said anywhere. Without the scheduling secret,
  automatic backups and scheduled exports were rejected exactly as a forged
  request would be, so they never ran and the logs read like a credentials
  problem.

- **Rate limiting by address is materially more reliable.** In several common
  setups every visitor shared a single limit, so one person's failed sign-ins
  could lock out everybody. The trusted-proxy list is also read properly now:
  IPv6 addresses match however they are written, an address with a port attached
  is handled, and entries that were never supported are reported rather than
  ignored in silence.

## Upgrading

**Only if you email scheduled reports through a server with a self-signed or
otherwise untrusted certificate.** Certificate checking used to be off for
everyone, so such an installation needs one change after this update.

The symptom is scheduled mail stopping, with the error *"Could not connect to the
configured host and port"*. Either install a trusted certificate on the mail
server, or go to **Admin → Scheduled Exports**, edit the SMTP credential, tick
**Allow self-signed certificate**, and save.

Everything else needs no action. A correctly configured system starts as before,
with one extra line in the log naming the proxy addresses it trusts — worth
reading once against your actual network setup. A small number of rate-limit
counters reset on the first start after upgrading.
